ddx.step1_summary:
- Chief complaint: Painful, cracked, itchy skin on the palms of both hands
- Onset/duration: Began ~3–4 months ago; progressively worsened to impair work over last days
- Severity/impact: Significant pain and cracking; unable to work for past 3 days
- Location: Primarily palms; patient notes mild generalized dryness (e.g., legs) but not severe
- Character: Dryness, fissuring/cracking, intermittent itch; occasional bleeding only after scratching
- Aggravating/alleviating factors: Occupational exposure to cleaning products; inconsistent glove use; OTC emollient (E45) not helpful; oral antihistamine not helpful
- Associated symptoms: Denies fever, GI or urinary symptoms; otherwise feels well; appetite intact
- Past medical history: Type 2 diabetes mellitus
- Medications: Metformin
- Allergies: No known drug or general allergies
- Family history: Diabetes; no known skin disease, asthma, or IBD
- Social/occupational: Housekeeper at a hotel; frequent exposure to cleaning chemicals; inconsistent glove use; nonsmoker; minimal alcohol
- Exam/vitals: Not provided in transcript
- Labs/imaging: None mentioned

I: Tinea manuum (dermatophyte infection): Chronic itchy scaling/cracking of hands can be fungal; occupational wet work may predispose; however distribution and lack of classic features make it less likely.
Scabies: Can cause pruritic hand involvement (especially interdigital), but absence of nocturnal itch, burrows, or household spread argues against.
D: Asteatotic/xerotic eczema: Baseline generalized dry skin, possibly worsened by low hydration and frequent washing; diabetes can contribute to xerosis.
Diabetic cheirodermatopathy (limited joint mobility/waxy skin): Diabetes-related hand skin changes, though typically with tight, waxy skin rather than itchy fissuring.
I2: Irritant contact dermatitis (wet work/cleaning chemicals): Strong temporal relation to new hotel housekeeping job, frequent exposure to detergents/disinfectants, inconsistent glove use; classic for painful, cracked, itchy palms.
Irritant dermatitis from frequent hand washing/sanitizers: Repeated water/soap/alcohol exposure disrupts barrier and causes fissuring.
A: Allergic contact dermatitis (e.g., to cleaning agents, fragrances, preservatives, rubber accelerators): Occupational exposure with pruritic hand dermatitis fits; may coexist with irritant dermatitis.
Dyshidrotic eczema (pompholyx): Pruritic hand eczema often on palms/sides of fingers; can fissure chronically, sometimes triggered by irritants.
Palmoplantar psoriasis: Can present with hyperkeratotic, fissured palms; usually less pruritic and often with other psoriatic stigmata.
T: Mechanical irritant/chapping from friction and abrasion during cleaning: Physical trauma can exacerbate hand eczema and fissuring.
E: Hypothyroidism: Can cause generalized xerosis; no other hypothyroid symptoms reported but could contribute.
Diabetes-related xerosis: Diabetes predisposes to dry skin and impaired barrier/repair.

step3_ranked_ddx.diagnosis: Irritant contact hand dermatitis (wet work/cleaning chemicals)
step3_ranked_ddx.explanation: Classic presentation of occupational hand dermatitis with strong temporal link to new job, repeated exposure to chemical irritants, and inconsistent glove use, leading to painful, cracked, itchy palms.
supporting_evidence: Onset after switching to hotel housekeeping ~3–4 months ago
Frequent exposure to cleaning products and wet work; admits not always wearing gloves
Palmar-dominant dryness, fissuring, pain and itch typical of irritant hand dermatitis
No systemic symptoms; antihistamine ineffective (non-histamine-mediated process)
Emollient alone (E45) not sufficient, consistent with active irritant inflammation
opposing_evidence: Mild generalized dryness could suggest a constitutional component beyond pure irritant exposure
No direct observation of erythema or dermatitis morphology on exam (tele-visit context)

step3_ranked_ddx.diagnosis: Allergic contact dermatitis to occupational agents (e.g., fragrances, isothiazolinones, quats, rubber accelerators)
step3_ranked_ddx.explanation: Occupational hand eczema may be allergic or mixed; sensitization to cleaning agents or glove chemicals can mimic or coexist with irritant dermatitis.
supporting_evidence: Occupational exposure to multiple potential allergens in cleaning products
Pruritus present; chronicity fits sensitization time course
Palmar involvement common in hand ACD
opposing_evidence: No clear identification of a specific trigger or pattern (e.g., dorsum involvement, glove-related distribution)
Symptoms began soon after job change; allergic sensitization sometimes requires longer exposure
Antihistamine ineffective (though expected in eczematous ACD)

step3_ranked_ddx.diagnosis: Asteatotic/xerotic eczema (barrier dysfunction), exacerbated by diabetes and low hydration
step3_ranked_ddx.explanation: Baseline generalized dryness and diabetes suggest impaired skin barrier and repair; wet work can superimpose and worsen fissuring, especially on hands.
supporting_evidence: History of generalized dry skin (legs) and low fluid intake
Diabetes mellitus associated with xerosis and impaired skin healing
opposing_evidence: Marked localization to palms rather than typical shins/trunk distribution
Temporal association with new occupational exposures is stronger for contact dermatitis

step3_ranked_ddx.explanation: Pruritic eruptions on palms can fissure chronically; can be triggered by irritants and wet work.
supporting_evidence: Palmar pruritus and chronic hand eczema
opposing_evidence: No mention of characteristic vesicles or blistering on sides of fingers/palms
Pain from fissures predominates rather than episodic vesicular flares

step3_ranked_ddx.diagnosis: Tinea manuum (dermatophyte infection of the hand)
step3_ranked_ddx.explanation: Can cause chronic pruritic scaling and fissuring of the hand, but transcript lacks typical features and risk markers.
supporting_evidence: Chronic hand symptoms with itch and fissuring
opposing_evidence: No unilateral predominance or classic scaling described
No mention of tinea pedis/onychomycosis (common concurrent sites)
Lack of response to emollients is nonspecific; no antifungal tried
